keyPhrase: ITA Section 37(12) SR&ED late filing penalty
description: Understand consequences of missed deadlines under Canada's ITA Section 37(12) legislation, including the SR&ED late filing penalty and disallowed claims.
summary: This page explains the SR&ED late-filing rules under Canada's Income Tax Act for taxpayers claiming SR&ED expenditures and investment tax credits. Corporations must file Form T661 and Schedule T2SCH31 within 18 months of taxation year-end; the deadline cannot be extended, taxpayer relief cannot revive a late claim, and unclaimed amounts are permanently lost.

body.text: This page explains the SR&ED late-filing rules under Canada's Income Tax Act for taxpayers claiming SR&ED expenditures and investment tax credits. Corporations must file Form T661 and Schedule T2SCH31 within 18 months of taxation year-end; the deadline cannot be extended, taxpayer relief cannot revive a late claim, and unclaimed amounts are permanently lost.

Canada’s research and development (R&D) tax incentive architecture—anchored federally by the Scientific Research and Experimental Development (SR&ED) Tax Incentive Program under the Income Tax Act (R.S.C., 1985, c. 1 (5th Supp.)) and the Income Tax Regulations (C.R.C., c. 945)—has undergone its most consequential statutory transformation in over a decade. Following policy proposals introduced in the 2024 Fall Economic Statement (tabled December 16, 2024) and expanded in the 2025 Federal Budget, Parliament enacted Bill C-15 (Budget 2025 Implementation Act, No. 1, S.C. 2026, c. 3), which received Royal Assent on March 26, 2026. Effective retroactively for taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024, Bill C-15 doubled the annual expenditure limit for the enhanced 35% refundable Investment Tax Credit (ITC) from $3 million to $6 million (increasing the maximum annual federal cash refund on current expenditures from $1.05 million to $2.1 million), broadened the prior-year taxable capital phase-out range from $10 million–$50 million to $15 million–$75 million, extended access to the 35% enhanced refundable ITC to Eligible Canadian Public Corporations (ECPCs) for the first time, and reinstated the eligibility of capital expenditures, shared-use equipment (SUE), and equipment lease costs incurred after December 15, 2024. Furthermore, effective April 1, 2026, the Canada Revenue Agency (CRA) launched an elective Pre-Claim Approval Process that halves post-filing expenditure review service standards from 180 calendar days to 90 calendar days, while Budget 2026 (tabled November 5, 2026) proposed further expansions covering regulatory certification and intellectual property (IP) registration costs alongside administrative streamlining of corporate tax elections.

At the sub-national level, provincial and territorial R&D tax incentives have simultaneously evolved, creating a multi-layered fiscal environment where combined federal and provincial refundable tax credits can recover a substantial portion of eligible R&D labour and capital outlays. Most notably, Québec replaced its legacy suite of provincial R&D tax credits with the consolidated Tax Credit for Research, Innovation and Commercialization (CRIC) for taxation years beginning after March 25, 2025, offering a 30% refundable credit on the first $1 million of eligible R&D and pre-commercialization expenditures above an exclusion threshold and 20% refundable on the excess. Concurrently, practitioner analyses of British Columbia’s Budget 2026 report that the province made the 10% BC SR&ED Tax Credit permanent (eliminating its former August 31, 2027 sunset clause) and harmonized its refundable expenditure limit at $6 million for taxation years beginning on or after December 16, 2024.
1. Executive Summary & Program Scale

The Scientific Research and Experimental Development (SR&ED) Tax Incentive Program is the single largest federal source of financial support for industrial innovation in Canada. Administered jointly in policy design by the Department of Finance Canada and in operational execution, scientific review, and financial audit by the Canada Revenue Agency (CRA), the program delivers dual statutory benefits to qualifying taxpayers carrying on R&D in Canada. First, under section 37 of the Income Tax Act, taxpayers may pool allowable current SR&ED expenditures—and, for property acquired after December 15, 2024, allowable capital SR&ED expenditures—under subsection 37(1) to deduct against net income for tax purposes in the current taxation year or carry forward indefinitely to offset taxable income in future taxation years. Second, under sections 127 and 127.1 of the Income Tax Act, taxpayers earn Investment Tax Credits (ITCs) calculated as a specified percentage (35% enhanced rate or 15% basic rate) of their SR&ED qualified expenditure pool under subsection 127(9), which may reduce federal Part I tax payable, be refunded directly in cash under section 127.1, or be carried back 3 taxation years and carried forward up to 20 taxation years under subsection 127(5).

CRA program statistics cited in 2026 industry analyses underscore the macroeconomic scale and high approval trajectory of the regime. During fiscal year 2024–2025, the CRA delivered $4.5 billion in SR&ED ITCs across more than 22,000 processed claims supporting over 19,000 distinct claimants. For the fiscal year ended March 31, 2026, total ITCs claimed rose to $4.9 billion, with $4.6 billion formally allowed by the CRA—representing an expansion of roughly 50% in annual credit value since fiscal year 2022. Contrary to widespread industry perceptions that SR&ED claims face prohibitive disallowance rates, CRA administrative data reported for the most recent cycle indicates that roughly 96% of all SR&ED claims result in allowed tax credits: specifically, 90% of claims are accepted as filed, 6% are accepted following technical or financial modifications, and 4% (roughly 1 in 25 claims) are denied in their entirety.

body.text: 2. Federal Statutory Architecture & The Definition of SR&ED
2.1 The Tripartite Statutory Framework of the Income Tax Act

A rigorous technical audit of any Canadian R&D tax claim requires separating three distinct statutory operations under the Income Tax Act (ITA). The first step is determining whether the underlying scientific or technological activity satisfies the legal definition of SR&ED under subsection 248(1). The second step is determining whether the expenditures incurred on that activity qualify for inclusion in the deductible SR&ED expenditure pool under section 37 and Part XXIX of the Income Tax Regulations (specifically section 2900). The third step is computing the qualified expenditures and resulting Investment Tax Credit under sections 127 and 127.1, after excluding prescribed expenditures under Regulation 2902 and deducting assistance and contract payments under subsections 127(11.1) and 127(18).

Practitioners and claimants frequently conflate these provisions—for instance, erroneously citing section 127 for activity eligibility or citing subsection 37(2) for assistance reductions. Under Canadian tax law, activity eligibility is governed strictly by subsection 248(1), whereas section 127 governs how qualified expenditures and tax credits are computed once technical eligibility is established. Similarly, subsection 37(2) deals exclusively with research carried on outside Canada (which is deductible against income but does not generate an ITC on the same basis, save for limited permissible foreign salaries under subsections 37(1.4) and 37(1.5)), whereas dollar-for-dollar reductions for government assistance, non-government assistance, and contract payments are governed by paragraph 37(1)(d) for the deduction pool and subsections 127(11.1) and 127(18) for qualified expenditures and ITC calculations.
2.2 Verbatim Analysis of Subsection 248(1): Eligible Core Work, Support Work, and Statutory Exclusions

Subsection 248(1) of the Income Tax Act defines "scientific research and experimental development" in general conformity with the OECD Frascati Manual while imposing strict domestic statutory boundaries. Under subsection 248(1), SR&ED means a systematic investigation or search that is carried out in a field of science or technology by means of experiment or analysis. The statutory definition is structured into three core qualifying categories (paragraphs (a), (b), and (c)), one conditional support work category (paragraph (d)), and seven explicit activity exclusions (paragraphs (e) through (k)):

items: Paragraph 248(1)(a) — Basic Research: Work undertaken for the advancement of scientific knowledge without a specific practical application in view.
Paragraph 248(1)(b) — Applied Research: Work undertaken for the advancement of scientific knowledge with a specific practical application in view.

Paragraph 248(1)(c) — Experimental Development: Work undertaken for the purpose of achieving technological advancement for the purpose of creating new, or improving existing, materials, devices, products, or processes, including incremental improvements thereto. In Canadian industrial practice, the vast majority of corporate SR&ED claims are filed under paragraph (c), including "shop-floor SR&ED" where experimental development takes place alongside commercial manufacturing or software engineering.

Paragraph 248(1)(d) — Eligible Support Work: Work undertaken by or on behalf of the taxpayer with respect to only eight enumerated disciplines—namely engineering, design, operations research, mathematical analysis, computer programming, data collection, testing, or psychological research—where the work is commensurate with the needs, and directly in support, of work described in paragraph (a), (b), or (c) that is undertaken in Canada by or on behalf of the taxpayer.
Paragraph 248(1)(e) — Excluded Work: Market research or sales promotion.
Paragraph 248(1)(f) — Excluded Work: Quality control or routine testing of materials, devices, products, or processes.
Paragraph 248(1)(g) — Excluded Work: Research in the social sciences or the humanities.
Paragraph 248(1)(h) — Excluded Work: Prospecting, exploring, or drilling for, or producing, minerals, petroleum, or natural gas.
Paragraph 248(1)(i) — Excluded Work: The commercial production of a new or improved material, device, or product, or the commercial use of a new or improved process.
Paragraph 248(1)(j) — Excluded Work: Style changes.
Paragraph 248(1)(k) — Excluded Work: Routine data collection.

body.text: Support work under paragraph 248(1)(d) cannot qualify in isolation; if there is no underlying core basic research, applied research, or experimental development under paragraphs (a), (b), or (c), none of the eight support categories can generate an eligible claim. Furthermore, as the CRA’s Guidelines on the Eligibility of Work for SR&ED Tax Incentives explain, the decisive factor distinguishing eligible support work under paragraph (d) (such as data collection or testing) from excluded work under paragraphs (f) or (k) (such as routine testing or routine data collection) is purpose. When data collection or testing is carried out specifically and exclusively to test a hypothesis aimed at resolving a scientific or technological uncertainty, and its scale is commensurate with those experimental needs, it qualifies as support work under paragraph (d). Conversely, if the same activity is undertaken for commercial compliance, production verification, or general business analytics, it is statutorily excluded under paragraphs (f) or (k).
2.3 Evolution of CRA Administrative Guidance: From IC 86-4 and the Five Questions to the "Why and How" Framework

To audit or prepare an SR&ED claim effectively, tax professionals must understand the historical progression of CRA administrative doctrine and its relationship to binding jurisprudence. Prior to 1985, administrative guidance regarding eligible "applied or basic research" or "development" was delivered through Interpretation Bulletin IT-439, which taxpayers and practitioners found insufficient to distinguish routine engineering from eligible R&D. In the May 1985 Budget Papers, the Department of Finance announced plans to amend the definition to introduce the term "experimental development," explicitly excluding projects involving only routine engineering or routine development. On March 4, 1986, the Department of Finance confirmed to Revenue Canada that qualifying activities must embody scientific or technological advancement, contain elements of scientific or technological uncertainty, and be carried out in a systematic and organized fashion.

Later in 1986, Revenue Canada and industry leaders co-developed Information Circular 86-4 (Scientific Research and Experimental Development, subsequently revised as IC 86-4R3 in 1994), which codified the Three Classic Criteria: (1) scientific or technological advancement, (2) scientific or technological uncertainty, and (3) scientific and technical content. In 1992, further clarification emphasized that experimental development must be undertaken for the purpose of achieving technological advancement to create or improve materials, devices, products, or processes. In 1998, Chief Justice Bowman’s landmark ruling in Northwest Hydraulic Consultants Ltd. v. The Queen (98 DTC 1839) synthesized IC 86-4R3 and the statutory text of subsection 248(1) into a five-part judicial test.

From 2012 to August 2021, the CRA’s Eligibility of Work for SR&ED Investment Tax Credits Policy (revised in 2015) directly mirrored the Northwest Hydraulic common law test by framing eligibility around Five Questions: (1) Was there a scientific or a technological uncertainty? (2) Did the effort involve formulating hypotheses specifically aimed at reducing or eliminating that uncertainty? (3) Was the overall approach adopted consistent with a systematic investigation or search, including formulating and testing the hypotheses by means of experiment or analysis? (4) Was the overall approach undertaken for the purpose of achieving a scientific or a technological advancement? and (5) Was a record of the hypotheses tested and the results kept as the work progressed?

On August 13, 2021, following a 2020 modernization review, the CRA archived the 2015 policy and published the Guidelines on the Eligibility of Work for SR&ED Tax Incentives, consolidating the five questions into two overarching requirements derived from subsection 248(1): the "Why" requirement and the "How" requirement. The "Why" requirement encompasses Questions 1 and 4 of the former policy, asking whether the work was conducted to advance scientific knowledge or achieve a technological advancement. Because recognizing a scientific or technological uncertainty marks the starting point of SR&ED and achieving an advancement is the targeted outcome, any systematic attempt to resolve a genuine scientific or technological uncertainty constitutes an attempt to achieve an advancement. The "How" requirement encompasses Questions 2, 3, and 5 of the former policy, asking whether the work was conducted by means of a systematic investigation or search in a field of science or technology by means of experiment or analysis. Under the CRA guidelines, satisfying the "How" requirement demands four operational elements: (1) generating an idea (hypothesis) consistent with known facts as a starting point for investigation; (2) testing that idea or hypothesis through experiment or analysis (allowing the hypothesis to evolve as testing progresses); (3) developing logical conclusions based on the experimental or analytical findings; and (4) keeping contemporaneous evidence generated as the work progresses. As the Federal Court of Appeal confirmed in National R&D Inc. v. Canada (2022 FCA 72) and Kam-Press Metal Products Ltd. v. Canada (2021 FCA 88), the CRA’s "Why and How" framework is strictly an administrative communication tool and does not alter the statutory definition in subsection 248(1) or supersede the binding five-part common law test in Northwest Hydraulic.
3. Enacted Federal Legislative Reforms (2024–2026)
3.1 From the 2024 Fall Economic Statement to Bill C-15 (Royal Assent: March 26, 2026)

When auditing or preparing SR&ED claims for taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024, tax practitioners must carefully distinguish between the initial legislative proposals announced in the 2024 Fall Economic Statement (FES 2024) on December 16, 2024, and the final statutory rules enacted by Bill C-15 (Budget 2025 Implementation Act, No. 1, S.C. 2026, c. 3), which received Royal Assent on March 26, 2026. In FES 2024, the Department of Finance originally proposed increasing the expenditure limit for the 35% enhanced ITC from $3 million to $4.5 million (which would have provided a maximum annual refundable credit of $1.575 million). However, Parliament dissolved before the FES 2024 legislation was enacted. In the 2025 Federal Budget, the government expanded the reform further, doubling the expenditure limit from $3 million to $6 million. Enacted into law via Bill C-15 on March 26, 2026, these enhancements apply retroactively to taxation years that begin after December 15, 2024, while the restoration of capital expenditures, shared-use equipment, and equipment lease costs applies to depreciable property acquired (and available for use) or lease costs incurred after December 15, 2024.
3.2 Doubling of the Enhanced Expenditure Limit ($6 Million) and Widened Phase-Out Thresholds ($15M–$75M)

For taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024, qualifying Canadian-Controlled Private Corporations (CCPCs) and Eligible Canadian Public Corporations (ECPCs) earn the enhanced 35% ITC (comprising the 15% basic rate under subsection 127(9) plus the 20% enhancement under subsection 127(10.1)) on qualified SR&ED expenditures up to an annual expenditure limit of $6,000,000. Because current SR&ED expenditures and the Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA) earned within the expenditure limit are 100% refundable under section 127.1, the maximum annual federal cash refund available to an eligible corporation or associated corporate group has doubled from $1,050,000 to $2,100,000.

Under subsection 127(10.2), the $6,000,000 expenditure limit is shared across an associated corporate group (which must file an allocation agreement on Schedule T2SCH49 under subsection 127(10.3)) and is subject to a gradual phase-out based on prior-year corporate size. Historically, a CCPC’s expenditure limit began phasing out once its prior-year taxable capital employed in Canada (on an associated-group basis) exceeded $10 million and reached nil at $50 million. Under Bill C-15, the prior-year taxable capital phase-out thresholds have been widened to $15,000,000 and $75,000,000. A CCPC group with prior-year taxable capital of $15 million or less retains the full $6,000,000 expenditure limit; between $15 million and $75 million, the limit is reduced linearly ($1 of expenditure limit reduced for every $10 of taxable capital above $15 million), reaching nil once taxable capital reaches $75 million. Furthermore, to prevent venture-backed technology, biotechnology, and clean-tech start-ups with high equity/debt balances but low revenues from phasing out prematurely, Bill C-15 allows CCPCs to elect on the prescribed form to compute their expenditure limit reduction using the ECPC gross revenue method—which phases out the $6,000,000 limit linearly based on average annual gross revenue over the three preceding fiscal years between $15,000,000 and $75,000,000—instead of taxable capital.
3.3 Extension of the 35% Refundable ITC to Eligible Canadian Public Corporations (ECPCs)

In a landmark structural shift, Bill C-15 amended subsection 127(9) to extend the 35% enhanced refundable ITC on up to $6,000,000 of qualified SR&ED expenditures to Eligible Canadian Public Corporations (ECPCs) for taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024. To qualify as an ECPC throughout a taxation year under subsection 127(9), a corporation must satisfy one of two statutory definitions. Under the first definition, the corporation must, throughout the taxation year: (1) be resident in Canada; (2) have a class of shares listed on a designated stock exchange (or have elected, or been designated by the Minister of National Revenue, to be a public corporation); and (3) not be controlled directly or indirectly in any manner whatsoever by one or more non-resident persons. Under the second definition, the corporation must be a Canadian-resident corporation where all or substantially all (90% or more) of the shares of its capital stock are owned by one or more eligible Canadian public corporations described in the first definition.

Unlike CCPCs, which default to the taxable capital phase-out unless they elect the revenue alternative, ECPCs are required to have their $6,000,000 expenditure limit reduced based on their average annual gross revenue over the three preceding fiscal years between $15,000,000 and $75,000,000. Within its available expenditure limit, an ECPC receives a 100% cash refund on its 35% ITC earned on current expenditures and PPA, and a 40% cash refund on its 35% ITC earned on eligible capital expenditures. Any qualified expenditures of an ECPC exceeding its expenditure limit earn the basic 15% ITC on a non-refundable basis.

body.text: 3.4 Reinstatement of Capital Expenditures, Shared-Use Equipment (SUE), and Lease Costs (Post-December 15, 2024)

Between January 1, 2014 and December 15, 2024, capital expenditures (depreciable property), shared-use equipment, and equipment lease payments were excluded from SR&ED deductions and ITCs following the 2012 Federal Budget repeal. Bill C-15 reversed that policy for depreciable property acquired (and available for use) and lease costs incurred after December 15, 2024, restoring three distinct capital and leasing pathways as detailed in the CRA’s updated SR&ED Capital Expenditures Policy (updated June 29, 2026), SR&ED Shared-Use Equipment Policy (updated May 22, 2026), and SR&ED Lease Expenditures Policy (updated June 8, 2026).

Under the first pathway—All or Substantially All (ASA) Capital Expenditures governed by paragraph 37(1)(b), subsection 37(1.2), and subclauses 37(8)(a)(ii)(A)(III) and (B)(III)—depreciable property (as defined in subsection 13(21), meaning property owned by the claimant for which Capital Cost Allowance [CCA] could otherwise be claimed) acquired after December 15, 2024 qualifies if, at the time of acquisition, the claimant intended either to use the property during all or substantially all (ASA, meaning 90% or more) of its operating time in its expected useful life in the prosecution of SR&ED carried on in Canada, or to consume ASA (90% or more) of its value in the prosecution of SR&ED carried on in Canada. Qualifying ASA capital expenditures are claimed on Line 390 of Form T661 (with the 10 most expensive properties per project listed on Lines 262 and 263 and the 20 most expensive listed in Box 780) and enter the Section 37 deductible expenditure pool, permitting a 100% write-off against taxable income in the year the asset becomes available for use (which precludes claiming regular CCA on Schedule T2SCH8 and deems the deducted amount to be CCA for recapture purposes). While both new and used depreciable property meeting the 90% ASA intent test can be deducted in the Section 37 pool, used property is excluded from earning an SR&ED Investment Tax Credit unless refurbished by a vendor so extensively that it is considered "new" when acquired (or limited to the claimant's own post-acquisition refurbishment expenditures). For CCPCs and ECPCs earning the 35% enhanced ITC on eligible new capital expenditures, the ITC is partially refundable at a rate of up to 40% (yielding an immediate cash refund equal to 14% of the capital cost—40% of the 35% credit—with the remaining 21% credit available to reduce Part I tax or carry forward). Land, leasehold interests in land, inventory, goodwill, buildings, and leasehold interests in buildings are strictly excluded from SR&ED capital expenditures under paragraphs 37(8)(d) and (e) (save for prescribed special-purpose buildings approved under Regulation 2903), and General Purpose Office Equipment or Furniture (GPOEF) is excluded when the claimant elects the Proxy Method.

Under the second pathway—Shared-Use Equipment (SUE) governed by subsection 127(9) and Regulation 2900(11)—new depreciable property acquired and available for use after December 15, 2024 that does not meet the 90% ASA test because it is used for both SR&ED and commercial activities may still earn ITCs on Line 504 of Form T661 (with the 20 most expensive SUE items listed in Part 6, including Box 792). To qualify as SUE, the equipment must be new, must not be GPOEF, and must not be Prescribed Depreciable Property (PDP) under Regulation 2900(11). Under paragraphs 2900(11)(c) and (d), equipment is excluded as PDP if, at the time of acquisition, the claimant intended to use it for SR&ED during the assembly, construction, or commissioning of a commercial manufacturing/processing facility, plant, or line, or intended over its expected useful life to use it primarily for non-SR&ED purposes. Unlike ASA capital property, SUE is not included in the Section 37 deductible expenditure pool; instead, the claimant depreciates the capital cost under regular CCA rules on Schedule T2SCH8 (and any SUE ITC applied or refunded reduces the class Undepreciated Capital Cost [UCC] in the subsequent taxation year). For ITC purposes, if actual SR&ED operating time is primarily (more than 50% but less than 90%) of total operating time during the First Period (starting at the time the property was acquired, rather than when it becomes available for use, and ending at the end of the first taxation year ending at least 12 months later), the equipment qualifies as First-Term SUE and 25% (1/4) of its capital cost is included as a qualified expenditure. If the asset qualified as First-Term SUE and actual SR&ED operating time remains more than 50% throughout the Second Period (starting at acquisition and ending at the end of the first taxation year ending at least 24 months later), it qualifies as Second-Term SUE and an additional 25% (1/4) of its capital cost is included as a qualified expenditure in that second year.

Under the third pathway—Equipment Lease Expenditures governed by paragraph 37(1)(a) and subclauses 37(8)(a)(ii)(A) and (B)—lease costs incurred after December 15, 2024 for the right to use equipment in Canada are restored to eligibility (reported in Box 759 and Lines 350, 355, or 360 of Form T661). When a claimant uses the Traditional Method, if leased equipment (including leased GPOEF) is used 90% or more (ASA) of its operating time in SR&ED, 100% of the lease cost is claimed on Line 350; if it is used less than 90% of the time in SR&ED, the proportional percentage of the lease cost that is directly attributable (directly related and incremental under Regulation 2900(2)(c)) to SR&ED is claimed as overhead on Line 360. Conversely, when a claimant elects the Proxy Method, GPOEF lease costs are completely excluded; for other leased equipment, 100% of the lease cost is claimed on Line 350 if SR&ED operating use is 90% or more (ASA), 50% of the lease cost is claimed on Line 355 if SR&ED operating use is primarily (more than 50% but less than 90%), and 0% is claimable if SR&ED operating use is 50% or less. Under both methods, lease payments for buildings remain excluded under paragraph 37(8)(d) and subparagraph 37(8)(e)(i), unless the building is a prescribed special-purpose building under Regulation 2903 or a non-building structure (such as a bridge or dam) meeting operational criteria.
3.5 Budget 2026 Measures (Tabled November 5, 2026) and Patent Box Status

On November 5, 2026, the Government of Canada tabled Budget 2026, introducing targeted legislative and administrative measures that further refine the R&D and capital investment regime. First, Budget 2026 proposes to expand eligible SR&ED activities and expenditures—with a projected federal fiscal cost of $930 million to $936 million over five years (2026–27: $25M; 2027–28: $200M; 2028–29: $245M–$247M; 2029–30: $225M–$227M; 2030–31: $235M–$237M)—to encompass certain commercialization activities conducted to meet regulatory or certification requirements for a product or process, as well as certain expenditures related to the registration and maintenance of intellectual property (IP) protection for IP developed through SR&ED. Litigation costs remain ineligible, and the measure applies to taxation years beginning on or after November 5, 2026.

Second, in its Tax Measures: Supplementary Information, Budget 2026 proposes to streamline SR&ED corporate tax filings by eliminating the requirement for corporations to submit a certified copy of a board of directors' resolution or authorization when making corporate elections or agreements to transfer qualified SR&ED contract expenditures (Form T1146) or allocate salaries and wages of specified employees (Form T1174), effective for elections and agreements made on or after Royal Assent of the enacting legislation. Third, to accelerate broader capital formation, Budget 2026 announced the Productivity Mega Deduction (an expansion of the Productivity Super Deduction with an estimated fiscal cost of $36.055 billion over five years, allowing permanent immediate expensing across more than 65% of business investment and reducing Canada’s Marginal Effective Tax Rate [METR] on new business investment from 13% to 6.4%) alongside the Canada Growth Incentive (providing a capital gains exemption on up to $15 million of capital gains from qualifying corporate shares). Notably, despite conducting stakeholder consultations in 2024 on establishing a preferential "Patent Box" or IP Box tax rate for income derived from Canadian-developed IP, the federal government did not include a Patent Box regime in either Budget 2025 or Budget 2026.
4. Qualifying SR&ED Expenditures (QREs) & Calculation Methodologies
4.1 The Election Between the Traditional Method and the Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA) Method

Under subsection 37(10) and clause 37(8)(a)(ii) of the Income Tax Act, a claimant must elect on Lines 160 and 162 of Form T661 whether to compute its SR&ED expenditures for the taxation year using the Traditional Method (clause 37(8)(a)(ii)(A)) or the Proxy Method (clause 37(8)(a)(ii)(B)). This election is made annually on a year-by-year basis when filing the original Form T661 for the taxation year; if no election is made, the Traditional Method applies automatically. Once Form T661 is filed for a given taxation year, the choice of method is statutorily irrevocable for that taxation year.

When a claimant elects the Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA) Method under subsection 2900(4) of the Income Tax Regulations, it does not specifically identify, track, or claim actual SR&ED overhead and other expenditures. Instead, the claimant computes a notional Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA) in Part 5 (Line 820) of Form T661 equal to 55% of the eligible proxy salary base. In any audit of Canadian R&D claims, it is critical to verify that the 55% rate is applied: assertions referencing a 65% or 60% overhead proxy rate reflect outdated law, as subsection 2900(4) set the rate at 65% up to 2012, 60% for 2013, and 55% since January 1, 2014. Because the PPA is a purely notional figure, it is excluded from the Section 37 pool of deductible SR&ED expenditures and is added solely on Line 502 of Form T661 to compute qualified SR&ED expenditures for the Investment Tax Credit (while the actual overhead expenses represented by the PPA remain deductible as ordinary business expenses under section 9(1) of the ITA). Under Regulation 2900(4) and Section B of Part 5 of Form T661, the PPA is also subject to an overall cap (computed via the formula A − B − C), which ensures that the notional proxy amount does not exceed total deductible business expenses net of specifically identified non-overhead deductions such as CCA, the Section 37 SR&ED pool deduction on Line 411 of Schedule T2SCH1, building rent, and interest.

Conversely, when a claimant uses the Traditional Method under Regulations 2900(2) and 2900(3), it claims actual SR&ED overhead and other current expenditures on Line 360 of Form T661, which enter both the Section 37 deductible expenditure pool and the qualified expenditure pool for ITC purposes. To qualify on Line 360 under paragraph 2900(2)(c), each overhead expenditure (or allocated portion thereof) must pass two mandatory cumulative tests in the CRA’s SR&ED Overhead and Other Expenditures Policy. First, under the "Directly Related" test, the expenditure must connect directly—without an intervening step or intermediary—to the SR&ED work, the SR&ED staff, or the machinery and equipment used by staff to perform SR&ED in Canada. Second, under the "Incremental" test, the expenditure must be one that would not have been incurred if the prosecution of SR&ED had not occurred (meaning fixed facility costs that do not vary with SR&ED activity fail the test, whereas variable utilities such as electricity, gas, and water consumed by SR&ED machinery or dedicated cloud compute instances qualify). While software and engineering teams with low physical overhead typically favour the simplicity and generous 55% uplift of the Proxy Method, the Traditional Method is advantageous for compute- or facility-intensive claimants—such as artificial intelligence firms training large models on AWS/GCP clusters or heavy industrial laboratories—where incremental cloud computing, variable shop-floor utilities, non-SR&ED support trade contracts (electricians, welders, mechanics), employer payroll benefits, and directly attributable support or supervisory salaries exceed 55% of the direct hands-on SR&ED salary base.

body.text: 4.2 Salaries and Wages: "Directly Engaged" Rules, Specified Employee Caps, and the 180-Day Unpaid Remuneration Rule

Allowable SR&ED salary or wages are governed by subsection 248(1) (which defines "salary or wages" as employment income computed under subdivision a of Division B of Part I—sections 5 to 8 of the ITA—excluding superannuation or pension benefits and retiring allowances), subsections 37(8), 37(9), and 37(9.1), and Regulations 2900(5) to 2900(10). Under the CRA’s SR&ED Salary or Wages Policy (updated January 28, 2025), whether an employee is "directly engaged" in SR&ED is a question of fact based strictly on the hands-on technical tasks performed rather than the employee's corporate title. Pursuant to Regulation 2900(5), if an employee spends all or substantially all (90% or more) of their working time throughout the taxation year directly engaged in SR&ED in Canada, 100% of their eligible salary or wages may be claimed. Where an employee spends less than 90% of their time on SR&ED, only the exact proportion of time devoted to hands-on SR&ED tasks—which may include short-term technological planning for ongoing claimed SR&ED projects, such as assigning technological personnel, setting job priorities, developing technological strategies, and assessing the quality of materials used—qualifies as permissible salary. Dividends paid to owner-managers, stock option benefits under section 7, extended vacation or sick leave, retiring allowances, and the employer's share of payroll benefits (CPP, QPP, EI, EHT—which are excluded from direct wages under both methods, though potentially claimable as overhead on Line 360 under the Traditional Method) are excluded from SR&ED salary or wages.

Stringent statutory limitations apply to any "specified employee," defined under subsection 248(1) as an employee who is a "specified shareholder" (owning, directly or indirectly at any time during the taxation year, 10% or more of the issued shares of any class of the corporation or a related corporation) or who does not deal at arm's length with the corporation (such as a spouse, sibling, or child of a controlling shareholder). First, whereas regular non-specified employees may have performance bonuses and profit-based remuneration included in direct SR&ED wages on Line 300 (though excluded from the PPA salary base under Regulation 2900(9)), subsection 37(9) strictly prohibits any bonus or remuneration based on profits paid to a specified employee from being claimed as an SR&ED expenditure. Second, under subsection 37(9.1), the maximum direct SR&ED salary claimable on Line 305 for a specified employee is capped at 5 times the Year's Maximum Pensionable Earnings (YMPE) for the calendar year in which the taxation year ends, prorated by the number of days in the taxation year the individual was a specified employee. Where a specified employee is employed by two or more associated corporations (or partnerships deemed to be associated corporations under subsection 37(9.5)), the group must file Form T1174 by the reporting deadline to allocate a single shared 5 × YMPE cap; failure to file Form T1174 on time deems the specified employee's SR&ED salary to be nil across all associated entities. Third, when calculating the proxy salary base in Part 5 of Form T661, Regulation 2900(9) first excludes taxable benefits (section 6), bonuses, profit-based remuneration, inducement payments, and prior-year unpaid wages paid in the current year (Line 310) for all employees; then, under Regulations 2900(7) and 2900(8), the proxy salary base for each specified employee (Lines 852–858) is capped at the lesser of 75% of the specified employee's total non-bonus salary or wages for the year (SR&ED and non-SR&ED combined) or 2.5 times the YMPE prorated by the number of days employed in the taxation year.

body.text: Two additional statutory rules govern geographic location and payment timing of SR&ED wages. Under subsections 37(1.4) and 37(1.5), while general foreign research costs under subsection 37(2) do not earn ITCs, a claimant may claim "permissible salary or wages" paid to Canadian-resident employees performing SR&ED work physically outside Canada on Line 307 (non-specified employees) and Line 309 (specified employees) of Form T661, provided the foreign work is integral to and solely in support of core SR&ED carried on in Canada and the wages are not subject to income or profits tax in the foreign country. The combined foreign salary claimed (Line 307 + Line 309) cannot exceed 10% of the total SR&ED salaries and wages incurred for work performed inside Canada (Line 306), and any amount claimed on Line 309 is limited to (10% × Line 306) minus Line 307. Finally, under subsection 78(4), any salary or wages incurred in a taxation year that remain unpaid on the 180th day after the end of the taxation year are deemed not to have been incurred in that year; they must be reported on Line 315 of Form T661 in the year incurred and can only be claimed on Line 310 in the subsequent taxation year when actually paid (at which point they are permanently barred from entering the proxy salary base under Regulation 2900(9)).
4.3 Materials Consumed vs. Materials Transformed (Subparagraph 37(1)(a)(i) & Regulation 2900(2)(a))

Under the CRA’s Materials for SR&ED Policy (updated March 27, 2026), "materials for SR&ED" means all physical, tangible raw materials, substances, or other items (in a solid, liquid, or gaseous state) that at a given moment in the SR&ED process compose the body of a tangible thing on which SR&ED is performed or that results from the SR&ED. General laboratory supplies that do not compose the body of the experimental object—such as petri dishes, beakers, flasks, pipettes, cleaning supplies, CDs/DVDs, used lubricants, or general utilities—do not qualify as materials for SR&ED, although under the Traditional Method they may qualify as overhead on Line 360 if directly related and incremental. Materials can only be claimed in the taxation year in which they are physically consumed or transformed in the prosecution of SR&ED in Canada (not when purchased into inventory), and the expenditure must be paid within 180 days of year-end to earn an ITC.

The statute and CRA policy distinguish sharply between materials consumed (Line 320 of Form T661) and materials transformed (Line 325 of Form T661). Materials consumed are materials that are destroyed, absorbed, broken down, or rendered virtually valueless (disposed of as waste or scrap with proceeds not exceeding 10% of cost) as a result of the SR&ED prosecution; they are 100% deductible and eligible for ITCs without recapture exposure. Materials transformed are materials that compose the body of a tangible object resulting from the SR&ED process (such as component parts incorporated into an experimental prototype, custom product, or commercial asset) that are not destroyed or rendered virtually valueless. While 100% deductible and eligible for ITCs in the year transformed, materials transformed are subject to ITC recapture under subsections 127(27) to 127(36) if the resulting property is sold or converted to commercial use within 20 taxation years.
4.4 Subcontractors (Arm’s Length vs. Non-Arm’s Length) and Third-Party Payments

When a claimant pays external parties to conduct SR&ED in Canada, eligibility and inclusion rates depend on whether the performer deals at arm's length with the claimant under section 251 and whether the arrangement is an SR&ED contract or a third-party payment. For arm’s length SR&ED contracts (Line 340 of Form T661), where a claimant pays an arm's length taxable supplier (a Canadian resident or a non-resident operating through a Canadian permanent establishment) to perform SR&ED in Canada on the claimant's behalf under subparagraph 37(1)(a)(i.01), 100% of the eligible contract expenditure enters the Section 37 deductible expenditure pool, but only 80% qualifies for the Investment Tax Credit under subsection 127(9). If a contract encompasses both Canadian and foreign R&D or both SR&ED and commercial work, only the portion reasonably allocated to SR&ED performed in Canada qualifies prior to applying the 80% ITC factor.

For non-arm’s length (NAL) SR&ED contracts (Line 345 of Form T661), where a payer contracts a related or affiliated entity to perform SR&ED, the payer's expenditure is deductible in its Section 37 pool, but is excluded from qualified expenditures under paragraph 127(9)(f) and earns $0 in ITCs for the payer (unless transferred). Instead, the NAL performer claims its own underlying SR&ED costs, and the amount received from the NAL payer is not treated as a "contract payment" grinding the performer's qualified expenditures. Under subsection 127(13), the NAL performer and NAL payer may jointly file Form T1146 (Agreement to Transfer Qualified Expenditures Incurred in Respect of SR&ED Contracts Between Persons Not Dealing at Arm's Length) to transfer all or part of the performer's qualified expenditures (capped at the contract amount) to the payer. Moreover, if an NAL contract is for support work only (paragraph 248(1)(d)), subsection 37(13) deems that linked work to be SR&ED in the hands of the NAL performer if it would have been SR&ED had the payer performed it directly, enabling the NAL performer to claim the costs or transfer them via Form T1146. Under the anti-avoidance rule in subsection 127(24), inserting an arm's length intermediary between an NAL payer and an NAL performer to obtain a qualified expenditure is disallowed.

Finally, third-party payments (Line 370 of Form T661 and Form T1263) under subparagraphs 37(1)(a)(i.1), (ii), and (iii) differ fundamentally from SR&ED contracts. Whereas under an SR&ED contract the payer controls the specifications of the work, is typically the sole funder, obtains exclusive rights to the SR&ED, and claims expenses on an accrual basis as work is performed, a third-party payment is a contribution made to an approved university, college, research institute, approved association, granting council, tax-exempt non-profit SR&ED corporation under paragraph 149(1)(j), or Canadian-resident corporation where the performer controls the R&D, multiple funders generally contribute, the claimant receives a non-exclusive right to exploit the results in its business, and the payment is claimed on a cash basis in the year paid (except for payments to Canadian-resident corporations under subparagraph 37(1)(a)(i.1), which follow accrual rules). Like arm's length contracts, third-party payments enter the Section 37 pool at 100% and earn ITCs on 80% of the eligible payment.
5. Assistance, Contract Payments, and Recapture Mechanics
5.1 Government Assistance, Non-Government Assistance, and Contract Payments (Subsections 127(11.1) and 127(18))

To ensure that Investment Tax Credits are earned only on a claimant's net at-risk R&D outlay, paragraph 37(1)(d) (governing the Section 37 deductible expenditure pool) and subsections 127(9), 127(11.1), and 127(18) (governing qualified expenditures and ITCs) require dollar-for-dollar reductions for any government assistance, non-government assistance, or contract payment in respect of SR&ED that the claimant has received, is entitled to receive, or can reasonably be expected to receive on or before the filing due date for the taxation year. Under the CRA’s Assistance and Contract Payments Policy, government assistance (subsection 127(9)) encompasses any grant, subsidy, forgivable loan, deduction from tax, or investment allowance provided directly or indirectly by a federal, provincial, municipal, or foreign government, Crown corporation, or public authority, other than the federal SR&ED ITC itself. This includes direct grants such as NRC IRAP contributions (reported on Line 515 of Form T661) and all provincial and territorial R&D tax credits (reported on Lines 513–517). While bona fide "excluded loans" with unconditional repayment obligations made after December 31, 2019 are excluded from government assistance under subsection 12(11), any forgivable or conditional loan whose repayment is contingent on project profits or commercial revenues is treated as assistance that reduces qualified expenditures immediately (with an ITC earned subsequently under subsection 127(10.7) only in the taxation year when the assistance is actually repaid).

Similarly, non-government assistance (subsection 127(9) and paragraph 12(1)(x)) includes any private inducement, reimbursement, grant, or allowance received to offset SR&ED costs, while a contract payment is an amount payable by an arm's length taxable supplier (or by a Canadian government, municipality, public authority, or tax-exempt entity) for SR&ED to be performed for it or on its behalf (reported on Lines 517 and 518). Where non-arm's length parties allocate assistance between themselves, they must file Form T1145 under subsections 127(19) and 127(20). When accounting for provincial R&D tax credits (such as the 8% Ontario Innovation Tax Credit) under the Proxy Method, the CRA’s Assistance and Contract Payments Policy enforces an important split: the portion of the provincial credit attributable to actual current expenditures reduces the federal Section 37 deductible expenditure pool under paragraph 37(1)(d), whereas the portion of the provincial credit attributable to the notional 55% Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA) does not reduce the Section 37 pool and is instead included directly in net income for tax purposes under paragraph 12(1)(x) on Schedule T2SCH1 in the year received.
5.2 Recapture of SR&ED Investment Tax Credits (Subsections 127(27) to 127(36))

Under subsections 127(27) to 127(36) of the Income Tax Act and the CRA’s Recapture of SR&ED Investment Tax Credit Policy, previously earned SR&ED ITCs are clawed back (added directly to Part I tax payable) if four cumulative conditions occur: (1) the claimant acquired a particular property (materials transformed, ASA capital equipment, Shared-Use Equipment, or property acquired through an arm's length SR&ED contract) in the current taxation year or in any of the 20 preceding taxation years (extended from 10 years to 20 years by subsection 127(36) for all ITCs earned in 1998 and subsequent taxation years); (2) the cost of the property was claimed as a qualified SR&ED expenditure; (3) an SR&ED ITC was earned in respect of that property; and (4) the claimant converts the property to commercial use or disposes of it (or disposes of/converts another asset incorporating the property).

The recapture addition to Part I tax under subsection 127(27) equals the lesser of: (a) the historical SR&ED ITC earned on the property, and (b) the historical ITC percentage rate (e.g., 35% or 15%) multiplied by the proceeds of disposition (if sold at arm's length) or the Fair Market Value (FMV) of the property at the time of commercial conversion or non-arm's length disposition. Crucially, in-house salaries, wages, and overhead are never subject to ITC recapture—even when incurred to fabricate a prototype or custom asset later sold commercially; only the cost of materials transformed (or purchased capital/contract property) is subject to recapture. Additionally, under the CRA’s 10% de minimis / scrap sale rule, if an experimental product or consumed material is sold as scrap for proceeds (or FMV) representing less than 10% of the total cost of the property (including salaries, overhead, and materials), no recapture is triggered.
5.3 Comprehensive Worked Mathematical Example: CCPC Under Post-Bill C-15 Rules (Proxy vs. Traditional Method & Provincial Stacking)

To demonstrate the exact statutory sequence for a 2026 taxation year under Bill C-15, consider Quantum Analytics Inc., an Ontario-based CCPC with $8,000,000 in prior-year taxable capital (below the $15,000,000 phase-out threshold, entitling it to the full $6,000,000 expenditure limit). During its taxation year ended December 31, 2026, Quantum incurs the following 100% Canadian SR&ED expenses on a single project:

items: Non-Specified Employee Salaries (100% hands-on SR&ED): $1,000,000 (consisting of $900,000 base salary and $100,000 performance bonuses).
Specified Employee Salary (Founder owning 40% of shares, working 100% on SR&ED for all 365 days of 2026): $250,000 regular salary plus a $50,000 year-end bonus ($300,000 total compensation).
Materials Consumed in SR&ED Testing (Line 320): $80,000.

Step 1 — Compute Allowable Direct SR&ED Salaries (Lines 300, 305, and 306): For the non-specified employees (Line 300), the full $1,000,000 (including the $100,000 bonus) qualifies as allowable SR&ED salary under subsection 37(8). For the specified employee (Line 305), subsection 37(9) disallows the $50,000 bonus entirely. The remaining $250,000 regular salary is tested against the 5 × YMPE cap under subsection 37(9.1): for 2026, YMPE is $74,600, yielding a cap of 5 × $74,600 = $373,000. Because $250,000 is below $373,000, the full $250,000 is allowable on Line 305, bringing total direct SR&ED salaries on Line 306 to $1,000,000 + $250,000 = $1,250,000.

Step 2 — Compute the Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA) Under the Proxy Method (Part 5 of Form T661): Under Regulation 2900(9), the $100,000 bonus paid to non-specified employees is stripped from the proxy salary base, leaving $900,000. For the specified employee (Lines 852–858), Regulation 2900(7) caps the proxy salary base at the lesser of: (a) 75% of total non-bonus salary (75% × $250,000 = $187,500), or (b) 2.5 × 2026 YMPE (2.5 × $74,600 = $186,500). The founder's proxy salary base is therefore capped at $186,500, resulting in a total proxy salary base (Line 815) of $900,000 + $186,500 = $1,086,500 and a 55% Prescribed Proxy Amount (Line 820 / Line 502) of 55% × $1,086,500 = $597,575.

6.1 The Absolute 18-Month Statutory Reporting Deadline (Subsections 37(11) and 127(9)(m))

Under subsection 37(11) (for SR&ED expenditures) and paragraph (m) of the definition of "investment tax credit" in subsection 127(9) (for SR&ED ITCs), a claimant must file the prescribed forms containing the prescribed information on or before the day that is 12 months after the claimant's income tax return filing due date for the taxation year in which the expenditures were incurred. Because a corporation's T2 income tax return filing due date under paragraph 150(1)(a) is 6 months after the end of its taxation year (and when a tax year ends on the last day of a month, the filing due date is the last day of the sixth month thereafter), the statutory SR&ED reporting deadline for a corporation is exactly 18 months after the end of the taxation year. Similarly, under subsection 127(26), any current expenditure (other than salary or wages) not paid within 180 days of year-end must be identified on Line 520 of Form T661 within this same 18-month reporting deadline or it can never be included in qualified expenditures when subsequently paid.

Following legislative amendments enacted in November 2005 (which removed ministerial discretion considered in earlier jurisprudence such as Alex Parallel Computers), the 18-month SR&ED reporting deadline is statutorily absolute. The Income Tax Act provides no mechanism to extend the deadline, and the taxpayer relief provisions in subsection 220(3.1) apply solely to waiving interest and penalties—they cannot revive a late-filed Form T661 or Schedule T2SCH31. As confirmed by the Tax Court of Canada in Easyway Cattle Co. Ltd. v. The Queen (2015 TCC 211) and Westsource Group Holdings Inc. v. The Queen (2017 TCC 9), if a claimant fails to file both Form T661 and Schedule T2SCH31 (or Form T2038(IND)) containing all prescribed project and financial line items on or before the 18-month deadline, the unclaimed SR&ED expenditures and ITCs are permanently lost.

body.text: 6.3 The Elective Pre-Claim Approval Process (Effective April 1, 2026) & CRA Service Standards

Effective April 1, 2026, the CRA launched its elective Pre-Claim Approval Process alongside AI-supported claim screening to provide upfront technical certainty and accelerate refunds. Before starting SR&ED work or incurring project costs, a business may submit an optional application via the SR&ED Client Portal for up to 3 projects, with each approval valid for up to 3 years. A meeting with a CRA Research and Technology Advisor (RTA) may be requested for existing claimants in good standing with the CRA and is mandatory for all other applicants. The RTA assesses whether the proposed project satisfies the subsection 248(1) definition of SR&ED (without auditing financial expenditures at the pre-claim stage) and issues a written determination within 8 weeks of receiving the completed application (note that there is no formal objection process if pre-claim approval is not granted, though the taxpayer may still file a regular year-end SR&ED claim).

Once a completed income tax return, Form T661, and Schedule T2SCH31 are filed, the CRA tracks three distinct processing service standards for refundable claims (there are no fixed service standards for non-refundable claims):

items: Within 60 Calendar Days: Refundable claims accepted as filed without a review.

Within 90 Calendar Days: Refundable claims selected for an expenditure-only review where the claim includes only projects that were granted Pre-Claim Approval—cutting review processing time in half from 180 days to 90 days.

Within 180 Calendar Days: Refundable claims selected for review that include any project not granted Pre-Claim Approval or materially differing from the pre-approved scope (targeted to be met 90% of the time).

body.text: 6.4 CRA Review Procedures, First-Time Claimant Advisory Service (FTCAS), and Penalties

Claimants submitting their first SR&ED claim—or those that have not filed an SR&ED claim in the preceding 3 years—may be selected for the First-Time Claimant Advisory Service (FTCAS), a mandatory educational service through which CRA specialists provide tailored recommendations to strengthen documentation and compliance for future claims. When a claim is selected for a technical and financial review under The SR&ED Review Process: A Guide for Claimants (updated July 2, 2025 / April 20, 2026), the review is executed jointly by a Research and Technology Advisor (RTA) (reporting to a Research and Technology Manager [RTM]) and a Financial Reviewer (FR) (reporting to a Financial Review Manager [FRM]). The review follows a structured three-step sequence:

items: Step 1 — Start of the Review: A reviewer contacts the claimant by telephone to introduce the assigned RTA and FR, confirm official language preference, identify the specific projects and technical/financial issues under review, schedule a virtual (or, exceptionally, on-site) review meeting, and follow up with an initial letter and meeting agenda (providing a standard 30-day timeline for pre-meeting information requests).

Step 2 — The Review Meeting & Information Requests: The RTA and FR interview the technical and financial leads, conduct a virtual or physical tour of the premises/equipment, and examine contemporaneous technical evidence (dated logs, test data, photographs, videos, prototypes, or scrap) and financial books and records (which must be retained for 6 years from the end of the taxation year under subsection 230(1) and paragraph 230(4)(b)). Under the CRA’s Claim Review Manual, RTAs are strictly prohibited from negotiating eligibility (they may never offer to accept one project in exchange for dropping another, nor accept an unsubstantiated percentage), and once a claim is selected for review, a claimant cannot withdraw the claim because the signed certification in Part 10 of Form T661 is an irrevocable part of the tax return.

Step 3 — End of the Review, Dispute Resolution & Objections: The RTA prepares the SR&ED Project Eligibility Report and the FR computes any resulting expenditure adjustments. If adjustments are proposed, the CRA issues a formal proposal package giving the claimant 30 days to submit written representations. Under the Guidelines for Resolving Claimants' SR&ED Concerns, unresolved disagreements follow a three-tier administrative escalation: (a) discuss with the RTA and/or FR; (b) escalate to the RTM and/or FRM; and (c) request an Administrative Review by the Assistant Director (who determines whether due process was accorded and whether the review complied with SR&ED legislation, policies, and procedures, issuing either a Decision Maintained or Decision Reconsidered letter). Following the issuance of a Notice of Assessment or Reassessment, the claimant has 90 days to file a formal Notice of Objection with the CRA Appeals Branch, and thereafter to appeal to the Tax Court of Canada.

body.text: Finally, under the CRA’s Gross Negligence Penalty on Overstated SR&ED Claims Policy (updated January 28, 2025, replacing Application Policy SR&ED 96-05), where a claimant knowingly, or under circumstances amounting to gross negligence, makes or participates in a false statement or omission on an SR&ED claim, penalties apply under subsection 163(2) of the Income Tax Act. As demonstrated in Les Éléments Chauffants Tempora Inc. v. The King (2025 TCC 173), Tempora (SCC 2018), and R. v. Elhami (2017 QCCQ 2684), fabricated dates or plagiarized technical narratives can reopen statute-barred taxation years and result in subsection 163(2) penalties or, on criminal conviction under section 239, fines ranging from 50% to 200% of the excess refund or credit claimed (100% to 200% on indictment).
7. Provincial and Territorial R&D Tax Credit Regimes

Ten Canadian jurisdictions (nine provinces and one territory: Alberta, British Columbia, Manitoba, New Brunswick, Newfoundland and Labrador, Nova Scotia, Ontario, Québec, Saskatchewan, and Yukon) provide dedicated R&D tax credits that stack with the federal SR&ED program, while Prince Edward Island, the Northwest Territories, and Nunavut do not offer a provincial/territorial R&D tax credit. All provincial and territorial R&D tax credits constitute "government assistance" under subsection 127(9) of the federal Income Tax Act and therefore reduce federal qualified SR&ED expenditures and the federal Section 37 deductible expenditure pool.
7.1 Ontario: OITC (8%), ORDTC (3.5%), and OBRITC (20%)

Administered by the CRA in harmonization with the Taxation Act, 2007 (Ontario), Ontario offers three distinct corporate R&D tax credits for corporations with a permanent establishment in Ontario. First, the Ontario Innovation Tax Credit (OITC) (Section 96 of the Taxation Act, 2007, claimed on Schedule 566 and reported on Line 468 of Schedule 5) provides CCPCs with an 8% fully refundable tax credit (reduced from 10% for taxation years starting after May 31, 2016) on up to $3,000,000 of qualified Ontario SR&ED expenditures per year (a maximum annual cash refund of $240,000), phasing out when prior-year associated-group taxable capital is between $25,000,000 and $50,000,000. Second, the Ontario Research and Development Tax Credit (ORDTC) (claimed on Schedule 508 and reported on Line 466 of Schedule 5) provides all corporations (CCPCs and non-CCPCs alike) with a 3.5% non-refundable tax credit (reduced from 4.5% for taxation years starting after May 31, 2016) on eligible Ontario SR&ED expenditures with no expenditure cap, a 3-year carryback, and a 20-year carryforward; corporations in a loss position may waive/renounce the ORDTC so it does not grind their refundable federal ITC. Third, the Ontario Business-Research Institute Tax Credit (OBRITC / OBTI) (Section 97 of the Taxation Act, 2007, claimed on Schedule 568 with Schedule 569 for each contract and reported on Line 470 of Schedule 5) provides a 20% fully refundable tax credit on qualified expenditures incurred in Ontario under an eligible contract with an eligible research institute, capped at $20,000,000 of qualified expenditures per year across an associated group (a maximum annual refundable credit of $4,000,000).
7.2 Québec: The Tax Credit for Research, Innovation and Commercialization (CRIC) (Effective After March 25, 2025)

Introduced in the 2025–2026 Québec Budget to replace the province's legacy RS&DE tax credits, the Tax Credit for Research, Innovation and Commercialization (CRIC) applies to taxation years beginning after March 25, 2025 for corporations that operate a business and maintain an establishment in Québec. Regardless of corporate size or taxable capital, the CRIC provides a fully refundable tax credit equal to 30% on the first $1,000,000 of qualified expenditures exceeding the applicable exclusion threshold, and 20% on all qualified expenditures above that $1,000,000 limit. For each taxation year, the applicable exclusion threshold equals the greater of $50,000 or the sum of the Basic Personal Amount (BPA) under the Québec personal income tax system for each employee, prorated to reflect the percentage of time spent by that employee on eligible R&D and pre-commercialization activities.

While Québec harmonizes its definition of R&D with federal subsection 248(1) (and relies on the CRA to perform the scientific review of R&D work), the CRIC expands provincial support to include pre-commercialization activities undertaken in Québec in conjunction with R&D work. Eligible pre-commercialization work encompasses: (1) tests, technological validations, and studies carried out to meet regulatory requirements aimed at obtaining an initial approval or certification to commercialize an innovation (including quality control activities only if they relate to implementing a quality control system required to obtain initial approval or certification); and (2) product design, including the development of form and aesthetics, improved functionality, and choice of materials. Qualified expenditures under the CRIC include 100% of salaries and wages paid to employees for eligible work in Québec, 50% of amounts paid to a subcontractor for a contract carried out in Québec, 50% of payments made to an eligible Québec public research centre, research consortium, or university entity, and 100% of property/equipment acquisition costs (excluding land, buildings, or rights to use land or buildings, and subject to a special recovery tax if the property ceases to be used solely in Québec within 730 consecutive days following the start of its use). Property claimed under the CRIC cannot be stacked with another Québec tax credit (such as the C3i credit) or claimed by a corporation holding a Large Investment Project tax holiday certificate for that project. To claim the CRIC, corporations file Form RD-1029.8.CR-T (and Form RD-1029.8.PR for pre-commercialization activities) with their Québec corporate income tax return.
7.3 British Columbia, Alberta, and Other Provincial/Territorial Regimes

In British Columbia, the BC SR&ED Tax Credit is administered jointly by the BC Ministry of Finance and the CRA on Form T666 (filed within 18 months of taxation year-end and reported on Line 674 for refundable credits and Line 659 for non-refundable credits on Schedule 5). According to a May 2026 practitioner guide, BC Budget 2026 made the 10% BC SR&ED Tax Credit permanent (eliminating its previous August 31, 2027 sunset date) and adopted the federal Bill C-15 enhancements for taxation years beginning on or after December 16, 2024. Consequently, CCPCs (and qualifying ECPCs) with a permanent establishment in BC earn a 10% fully refundable tax credit on up to $6,000,000 of qualified BC SR&ED expenditures (up to $600,000 in cash refunds per year), phasing out linearly when prior-year associated-group taxable capital is between $15,000,000 and $75,000,000. Expenditures above the $6,000,000 limit, as well as all qualified BC expenditures of non-CCPCs, earn a 10% non-refundable credit that can be carried back 3 years and carried forward 10 years.

In Alberta, the Innovation Employment Grant (IEG) (enacted effective January 1, 2021 under sections 26.95 to 26.99 of the Alberta Corporate Tax Act and detailed in Information Circular IEG-1) provides a refundable tax credit on up to $4,000,000 in annual Alberta R&D expenditures matching federal SR&ED eligibility. The IEG pays an 8% base rate on eligible Alberta R&D spending up to the corporation’s base spending level (defined as its average qualifying Alberta R&D spending over the preceding 2 taxation years) and an enhanced 20% rate on eligible Alberta R&D spending exceeding that 2-year average base. The grant phases out incrementally for corporations with prior-year taxable capital between $10,000,000 and $50,000,000 (reaching nil at $50,000,000) and is claimed on AT1 Schedule 29 (Form AT29) and Form AT4970 within 15 months after the corporation's filing due date.

Across the Prairie, Atlantic, and Northern jurisdictions, Manitoba provides a 15% R&D Tax Credit under section 7.3 of the Income Tax Act (Manitoba) on Schedule 380 (Line 613 and Line 606 of Schedule 5) with no expenditure cap, of which half (7.5%) is refundable for in-house R&D (100% refundable when conducted with eligible universities/colleges) and half (7.5%) is non-refundable (3-year carryback, 20-year carryforward; may be renounced within 6 months of year-end for federal purposes). Saskatchewan provides a 10% R&D Tax Credit on Schedule 403 (refundable for CCPCs on the first $1 million of eligible expenditures and non-refundable on the excess up to a $10 million total cap). Nova Scotia (Schedule 340), New Brunswick (Schedule 360), and Newfoundland and Labrador (Schedule 301 for corporations; Form T1129 for individuals) each provide a 15% fully refundable R&D tax credit with no expenditure cap, while Yukon (Schedule 442) provides a 15% fully refundable R&D tax credit (increasing to 20% on eligible payments to Yukon University).

body.text: 8. Federal Direct Grants & Clean Economy Investment Tax Credits
8.1 Direct Federal Innovation Grants (NRC IRAP, SIF, Global Innovation Clusters, Mitacs)

Canadian businesses frequently combine retrospective SR&ED tax credits with prospective direct government grants and contribution programs. The flagship federal grant program for small and medium-sized enterprises is the National Research Council of Canada Industrial Research Assistance Program (NRC IRAP), which provides non-repayable financial contributions toward technical salaries and contractor expenses for pre-approved innovation projects, alongside Youth Employment Programs and the IRAP Clean Technology Initiative proposed for renewal in Budget 2026. Receiving NRC IRAP funding does not disqualify a project from SR&ED; rather, the IRAP grant is reported as federal government assistance on Line 515 of Form T661, reducing only the specific expenditures subsidized while leaving the 55% Prescribed Proxy Amount on the full underlying direct SR&ED salary base intact. Larger commercialization and industrial R&D initiatives are supported through the Strategic Innovation Fund (SIF), Canada’s Global Innovation Clusters, academic internship partnerships through Mitacs, and the $750 million Early and Growth Stage Investment Strategy delivered through the Business Development Bank of Canada (BDC) under Budget 2026 ($75 million for pre-seed/seed companies and $675 million for later/growth-stage scale-ups).
8.2 Clean Economy Investment Tax Credits & Anti-Stacking Rules with SR&ED Capital Property

With the post-December 15, 2024 reinstatement of SR&ED capital expenditures, corporations investing in clean technology equipment must navigate the statutory interaction between Section 37/127 SR&ED capital claims and Canada’s refundable Clean Economy Investment Tax Credits. Under section 127.45 of the Income Tax Act (claimed on Schedule T2SCH75 and flowing to Line 155 of Schedule 31 and Line 780 of the T2 return), the Clean Technology (CT) Investment Tax Credit provides taxable Canadian corporations and eligible real estate investment trusts (REITs) with a 30% refundable tax credit (reduced by 10 percentage points to 20% if prevailing wage and apprenticeship labour requirements are not elected, except for off-road zero-emission vehicles and low-carbon heat equipment) on the capital cost of new eligible property in CCA Classes 43.1, 43.2, and 56 situated in and intended for use exclusively in Canada. Originally scheduled to step down to 15% in 2034 and expire after 2034, Budget 2026 proposed extending the Clean Technology and Clean Electricity ITCs to eligible property becoming available for use before 2041 and consulting on a domestic content bonus of up to 10 percentage points. Parallel credits include the Clean Technology Manufacturing (CTM) ITC, the Clean Hydrogen ITC, the Clean Electricity ITC, and the Carbon Capture, Utilization, and Storage (CCUS) ITC.

Crucially, under paragraph 127.45(9)(a) and corresponding Clean Economy ITC provisions, these capital credits are strictly mutually exclusive on a property-by-property basis: a taxpayer cannot claim two Clean Economy ITCs on the same asset, nor can a taxpayer claim both a Clean Economy ITC and an SR&ED ITC on the same property. However, a single facility or project containing multiple distinct pieces of capital equipment can segregate assets on a property-by-property basis—claiming SR&ED on experimental testing machinery used ≥90% ASA in R&D (35% enhanced rate, 40% refundable, plus 100% immediate Section 37 deduction) and the 30% fully refundable Clean Technology or CTM ITC on qualifying commercial clean technology assets.
9. Judicial Precedents & Audit Jurisprudence (1988–2026)

In Canadian tax litigation, the legal onus rests on the claimant to demolish the Minister’s factual assumptions through credible, contemporaneous evidence; being a first-time claimant does not lower this statutory burden. Over the past four decades, the Tax Court of Canada (TCC) and Federal Court of Appeal (FCA) have established a body of binding precedents that govern every CRA technical and financial review.
9.1 Foundational Jurisprudence: The Northwest Hydraulic Five-Part Test and Contemporaneous Evidence

In Sass Manufacturing Ltd. v. M.N.R. (88 DTC 1363 (TCC), 1988), the Tax Court established that a "systematic investigation" requires controlled, repeatable experiments, accurate measurements, and the testing of theories against empirical evidence where the steps, changes made, and results are carefully recorded. A decade later, in Northwest Hydraulic Consultants Ltd. v. The Queen (98 DTC 1839; 1998 CanLII 553 (TCC), 1998), Chief Justice Donald Bowman articulated the definitive five-criteria test for SR&ED eligibility (allowing 4 of the taxpayer's 5 hydraulic engineering projects). Judge Bowman established that technological uncertainty frequently arises at the system level even when individual components are known, and held that "although the Income Tax Act and the Regulations do not say so explicitly, it seems self-evident that a detailed record of the hypotheses, tests and results be kept, and that it be kept as the work progresses." Shortly thereafter, Rainbow Pipe Line Co. v. The Queen (96-4369-IT-G (TCC), 1999) confirmed that rejecting or disproving a hypothesis through systematic testing is itself a technological advancement because it eliminates a potential solution and advances technological understanding.

On the evidentiary threshold for contemporaneous documentation, the Federal Court of Appeal held in RIS-Christie Ltd. v. The Queen (99 DTC 5087 (FCA), 1999) and C.W. Agencies Inc. v. The Queen (2001 FCA 393; 2000 DTC 2372) that producing documentary evidence of repeatable tests recorded during the work is the primary reliable method of proving systematic investigation, and rejected retroactive conjecture by an external expert witness who had not participated in the software project. Only in narrow circumstances—such as the subsequent RIS-Christie round where the key engineer died prior to trial, or in Les Abeilles Service de Conditionnement Inc. v. The Queen (2014 TCC 313), where witnesses provided exceptionally credible, detailed oral testimony—have courts accepted oral evidence to overcome limited written documentation. Finally, on financial issues, Consoltex Inc. v. The Queen (97 DTC 724 (TCC), 1997) and Les Cultures Laflamme (1984) Inc. v. M.N.R. (89-2514(IT), 1989) confirmed the eligibility of experimental production runs later sold commercially (prompting the enactment of the subsections 127(27)–(36) ITC recapture rules), while Com Dev Ltd. v. The Queen (96-4343-IT-G (TCC), 1999) established that a commercial fixed-price deliverable contract where the vendor bears technical and financial risk is commercial revenue rather than a "contract payment" grinding SR&ED claims.
9.2 Standard Practice, Trial-and-Error, and Recent Appellate Rulings (2011–2026)

Subsequent appellate and trial decisions have policed the boundary between routine engineering / trial-and-error and experimental development. In Jentel Manufacturing Ltd. v. The Queen (2011 TCC 261; aff'd 2011 FCA 355) and Joel Theatrical Rigging Contractors (1980) Ltd. v. The Queen (2017 TCC 6), the courts confirmed that resolving complex mechanical design problems using standard engineering practice and existing techniques does not qualify as SR&ED. In 6398316 Canada Inc. v. The Queen (2021 TCC 17) (Global Sustainable), where the taxpayer built an off-grid energy-efficient home at a price comparable to a conventional house, Justice Russell held that "conceptually there is no technological aspect implicit in the notion of an item costing or priced at 'x' rather than 'y' dollars"—confirming that while business cost constraints provide context (as noted in National R&D, 2020 TCC 47), cost efficiency alone is an economic objective, not a technological uncertainty. And in National R&D Inc. v. Canada (2022 FCA 72) and Kam-Press Metal Products Ltd. v. Canada (2021 FCA 88), the Federal Court of Appeal confirmed that the CRA's August 2021 "Why and How" guidelines did not relax the scientific method rigour required under the Northwest Hydraulic test.

Between 2023 and 2026, the Tax Court of Canada issued landmark rulings across manufacturing, food science, and software engineering. In Buhler Versatile Inc. v. The King (2023 TCC 18) and Canafric Inc. v. The King (2023 TCC 108), taxpayers prevailed by demonstrating how mechanical sub-system integration (Buhler) and systematic root-cause analyses of formulation parameters (Canafric) met all five Northwest Hydraulic criteria. In Dazzm Inc. v. The King (2024 TCC 129), the Tax Court upheld a software claim involving cloud-based SaaS and open-source tool integration (React/Redux), ruling that systemic architectural and performance uncertainties must be evaluated holistically rather than dismissed as routine debugging. Conversely, in Vortex Energy Services Ltd. v. The King (2025 TCC 63) and Tuna Temple Inc. v. The King (2025 TCC 183), the Court dismissed claims founded on unrecorded trial-and-error prototyping and wages estimated equally across batches, while in Les Éléments Chauffants Tempora Inc. v. The King (2025 TCC 173), the Court held that plagiarized supplier/website text in technical reports constituted a misrepresentation reopening statute-barred years and supporting subsection 163(2) penalties. Most recently, in Willowglen Systems Inc. v. The King (2026 TCC 7), the Tax Court delivered a split decision that encapsulates modern software SR&ED law: it allowed the MTCLM SIL 4 train-control box project based on genuine cumulative system uncertainty not resolvable by available methods, but disallowed $1,293,692 for the SCADACOM-5 project because modernizing and scaling up software using known tools is commercial product development, not experimental development.
